My Black Vinegar lunch
Sep 2026 • Solo
We were happy to see that their Chinese Executive Chef Tony Guo has prepped the menu to include traditional Cantonese techniques and flavors with contemporary presentation, high-quality imported ingredients, and a distinct focus on "black vinegar" as a key element in their menu.

The Cuisine Style is Contemporary Cantonese, blending traditional Guangdong elements (dim sum, roasted meats, steamed seafood, delicate sauces) with modern flavor combinations and presentation. 

I view that the dishes are crafted to be flavorful yet light and not excessively oily, catering to the local Vietnamese and Chinese community's preference for clean, balanced Cantonese cuisine. 

We went through the paces of the a la carte lunch menu and chose a few significant dishes that represent the true DNA of Black Vinegar, and to assess their capability and culinary finesse. 

I tried the Cantonese Roast Duck with Five‑Spice & Tangerine Peel which presents itself with an amber-red gloss, its skin tight and crackling under the knife. 

The aroma is immediate: the warmth of five-spice mingled with the bright, almost fragrant note of tangerine peel, a subtle nod to traditional Cantonese home cooking, elegantly updated for the modern table

The first bite is all about contrast, and the skin shatters cleanly, releasing a whisper of fat that melts on the tongue, while the meat beneath remains juicy and deeply savory, marinated throughout rather than merely glazed on the surface. Superb! 

For the Stone Pot Braised Tofu with BBQ Pork Belly & Mushroom, it is part of the warm, comforting middle movement. Served bubbling in its clay pot, it releases a deep, caramelized aroma of soy, pork fat, and mushrooms that feels almost restorative. 

Due to the fact that I am a Cantonese food lover, I can attest to this brilliant quality. The tofu itself is the star: silky, custard-like blocks that have absorbed the braising liquid until they’re almost gelatinous at the edges, yet still tender within. 

Nestled among them are chunks of BBQ pork belly, their edges slightly charred and sweet, with fat rendered down to a soft, unctuous melt. 

The small earthy mushrooms cut to perfection, nicee… add a meaty chew and umami depth, while the well-mixed sauce - brown tangy colour, glossy, and reduced to a near-glaze—clings to every element. Spoonful after spoonful, the dish builds: salty-sweet pork, mellow tofu, forest-floor mushrooms, all bound by a sauce that tastes as if it’s been simmering for hours. It’s the kind of dish that makes the table fall silent for a moment, broken only by the sound of spoons scraping against the pot. Immaculate!

The dim sum medley arrives as a small parade of baskets, each piece a compact study in texture and flavor. Together, they trace a neat arc from bright seafood to rich, truffled earthiness

Shrimp Dumpling (Har Gow) with Fish Roe - The skin is nearly translucent, stretched thin enough to hint at the plump, snapping shrimp within. A scattering of fish roe on top adds tiny bursts of brine and a faint marine sweetness that elevates the simple purity of the prawn, always a key test for me at every Cantonese restaurant.

Pork Siu Mai with Scallop & Fish Roe - More robust than the har gow, this siu mai is juicy and pork-forward, but the minced scallop softens the texture and brings a gentle sweetness.

Cheese Beef Dumpling - A playful, modern twist. The beef is finely minced and well-seasoned, but it’s the melted cheese core that surprises..

Chicken Dumpling with Black Truffle - The chicken filling is delicate and clean, allowing the black truffle aroma to lead—earthy, musky, slightly garlicky.

Spinach Dumpling - The palate cleanser of the set; the spinach filling is bright, slightly bitter, and herbaceous, wrapped in a skin that often carries a faint green tint.
